title: Lab 11 — Quiz 2
subtitle: Unknown ID Part 2 — antimicrobials, Kirby-Bauer, Gram+ unknowns

questions.prompt: In Kirby-Bauer testing, what is measured, and in what units?

options.text: The radius of the zone, in centimeters
The number of colonies in the zone of inhibition
The diameter of the paper disc, in millimeters
The diameter of the zone of inhibition, in millimeters

questions.explanation: Diameter = visible growth to visible growth, in mm, then compared with the standards table.

why.B: The clear zone is measured, not counted.
why.C: The zone around the disc is measured.

questions.prompt: What agar is used for Kirby-Bauer testing?

options.text: MacConkey agar on a standard plate
Mueller-Hinton agar on an oversized plate
Blood agar on a standard plate
Mannitol salt agar on a standard plate

questions.explanation: Kirby-Bauer: pure culture, oversized Mueller-Hinton plate, a confluent 'lawn' of growth, antibiotic discs that diffuse into the agar.

why.D: MSA is for salt tolerance and mannitol.

questions.prompt: Azithromycin (AZM-15) standards: R ≤13 mm, I 14–17 mm, S ≥18 mm. Your zone measures 16 mm. Result?

options.text: Invalid — the zone must be measured in cm

questions.prompt: Penicillin (P-10) has no intermediate range: R ≤28 mm, S ≥29 mm. Your zone is 25 mm. Result?

options.text: Sensitive, since 25 mm is a large zone

questions.explanation: 25 mm ≤ 28 mm → Resistant. Zone sizes must always be compared with that drug's standards.

why.C: Each drug has its own cutoffs.

questions.prompt: A broad-spectrum antibiotic is best used when:

options.text: The pathogen is known and its sensitivity is known
The pathogen's identity or sensitivity is unknown
You want to protect the resident microbiota
You want the lowest risk of resistance

questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum: unknown pathogen or sensitivity, mixed infections, faster to give, often cheaper — but harms resident microbiota and has more resistance risk and adverse effects.

why.C: Broad-spectrum drugs also harm resident microbiota.
why.D: Broad-spectrum drugs carry a higher risk of resistance.

questions.prompt: Which is an ADVANTAGE of narrow-spectrum antibiotics?

options.text: They work well against mixed infections
Less harm to resident microbiota and lower risk of resistance
They can be given before any diagnosis

questions.explanation: Narrow-spectrum: minimize harm to resident microbiota, lower resistance risk, fewer adverse effects; need an accurate diagnosis.

why.A: Narrow-spectrum drugs are less effective against mixed infections.
why.C: An accurate diagnosis must be made first.
why.D: Narrow-spectrum drugs are often more expensive.

questions.prompt: Why does treating a helminth infection carry a greater chance of side effects?

options.text: The pathogen and patient are closely related eukaryotes, so selective toxicity is hard
Anti-helminthics are all broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs
Helminths make penicillinase that destroys the drug

questions.explanation: As the pathogen becomes more similar to the patient, selective toxicity gets harder.

why.C: They target worm metabolism, not bacteria.

questions.prompt: Beta-lactams (e.g., penicillin, methicillin) have high selective toxicity because they block:

options.text: Peptidoglycan synthesis, found only in bacteria

questions.explanation: Beta-lactams block cell wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis — a structure found only in bacteria.

why.A: Ribosome-targeting drugs have lower selective toxicity.

questions.prompt: Which antimicrobial is matched with its target?

why.B: Sulfa drugs inhibit folic acid synthesis.

questions.prompt: Which drug is an antifungal that inhibits ergosterol synthesis?
questions.explanation: Miconazole (Monistat) disrupts the fungal membrane by inhibiting ergosterol synthesis.

questions.prompt: A Gram-positive coccus is catalase positive, grows on MSA and turns it yellow, and is coagulase positive. Identify it.
questions.explanation: Catalase + → Staphylococcus; salt-tolerant + mannitol + (and coagulase +) → S. aureus.

why.A: S. epidermidis is mannitol and coagulase negative.
why.B: Streptococci are catalase negative and not salt-tolerant.

questions.prompt: A Gram-positive coccus is catalase negative, doesn't grow on MSA, and shows clear zones on blood agar. Identify it.
questions.explanation: Catalase − (Strep), not salt-tolerant, beta-hemolytic → S. pyogenes (Group A Strep; strep throat, skin and flesh-eating infections).

why.C: Staphylococci are catalase positive and salt-tolerant.

questions.prompt: Why is standardization of the Kirby-Bauer test critical?

options.text: Standardization makes every zone the same size
Zone sizes only mean R/I/S when conditions match the standard table
It allows any agar to be used
It removes the need for a pure culture

questions.explanation: Standardized features (pure culture, Mueller-Hinton agar, confluent lawn, disc concentrations, mm measurements) let zones be compared to the R-I-S table.

why.A: Zones differ by drug and organism.

questions.prompt: A '-static' antimicrobial differs from a '-cidal' one because it:
questions.explanation: '-cidal' kills; '-static' stops growth so the immune system can clear the microbe.

why.B: '-static' describes the effect, not the target.

questions.prompt: Polymyxins (polymyxin B, colistin) act by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Five targets: cell wall synthesis, cell membrane, protein synthesis, nucleic acid synthesis, folic acid synthesis.
